chapter_theme: Kuruntokai 301-320, mostly shore poems: the heroine sleepless at midnight (301, 302), pale or wasting (303, 316), stung by gossip she did not earn (311, 320), holding the man to his oath and the knotted bond (304, 313, 318); waiting through the rains and evenings (314, 319, 310); the paalai crescent and tusker (307); the friend's neythal that reblooms where it was weeded (309); and Kapilar's girl who is a thief of two faces (312).

iraicchi.act: the craving female calls out at midnight from the nest she shares with her mate
iraicchi.sense: the bird that has its mate beside it still calls for him, while the heroine, whose lover does not come, can only lie awake listening

comparisons.tenor: the sound in her ear of a chariot that is not coming
the palmyra's trunk, shaped like the base of a drum

301.reading: The heroine tells her friend that at midnight, when the pregnant female anril craving in its twig nest on the frond of the drum-trunked palmyra calls out, a sound rings in her ear as if the long chariot with its bells, cleaving the village common, were coming though it does not come, and her eyes have given up sleep.
301.nuance: The bird calls from inside a nest it shares with its mate, at the same hour that she lies alone; the chariot exists only as a sound her own ear makes, so the poem places the whole tryst inside her listening.

thinai_evidence.note: the palmyra and the anril of the shore village decide it against the colophon's kurinji

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: addressee from தோழி in line 8; stage inferred from the midnight chariot of a secret visit

302.reading: The heroine asks her friend whether it is not wrong: she can bear hard grief, but fears more that it may turn into something worse; alas, has the man of the good hill grown afraid of the gossip that says the two are inseparable, so that at midnight, when the town sleeps, he knows no way of coming except into her heart?
302.nuance: பெரும்பிறிது, the greater other thing, is left unnamed; it may be death or the end of the bond, and the poem's fear lives in the gap.

thinai_evidence.note: the man is of the good hill and the visit belongs to midnight

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: addressee from தோழி in line 1; stage from the gossip about the unmarried pair

303.reading: The friend tells the lord of the shore, where the black-legged white heron that has searched the backwater for food gathers in the thaazhai at the edge of the shore and sleeps through the roar of the breaking waves, that her friend, her bangles slipped from their old place, has grown pale here ever since the day she played with her, chasing the gold-striped crab in the spotted shade of the sweet-clustered punnai.
303.nuance: The heron that has fed and sleeps through the surf could be read as the man at ease while she wastes, but only one correspondence holds (his ease against her pain), so it fails condition 3 and stays scene; the crab game dates the pallor to the day of first meeting.

thinai_evidence.note: thaazhai, punnai and the shore crab

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: addressee from துறைவ in line 3; stage from the play-day meeting

304.reading: The heroine says that with the lord of the shore of cool kaithai waters, where, as the fishermen of curved boats hurl the sharp-mouthed harpoon on its strong shaft of dry bamboo at the horned fish in the unbearable sea, the white flock of short-legged swans sitting on the long shore scatters through the flowered grove, they have surely made a friendship that brings enmity.
304.nuance: The harpoon thrown at the shark scatters swans that were no part of the hunt; read as a hidden image it would make the lovers' bond scatter the innocent household, but no second pair can be fixed to the situation, so it stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: fishermen and kaithai of the shore

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: addressee inferred: the colophon gives only the speaker; she speaks of the man in the third person

comparisons.tenor: her love-sickness, which no one parts and which ends only in death
love as a fire that burns to the bone

305.reading: The heroine says the bright fire of love the eyes brought torments her to the bone, yet she cannot go to him and embrace him, nor does he come to remove her pain; they neither let go nor part, and like the lone fight of the dunghill cocks, which ends only when one dies, this sickness that has reached its height has no one to stop it.
305.nuance: The cocks fight on a rubbish heap with no one to part them; the image makes love-sickness a contest with no umpire, and 'ends only in dying' is said flatly.

thinai_evidence.note: the dunghill cock of the settled town is the poem's only native thing

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: addressee inferred: the colophon gives only the speaker

306.reading: The heroine asks her heart whether, though it said 'these are the soft, sweet, welcome, fitting words we shall speak', it will forget them once it has seen the lord of the cool sea, of the shore grove where bees fall on the pollen-filled flowers of the lovely mango.
306.nuance: The words may be the ones she means to say to him or the gentle words he once spoke; either way the heart's resolve is expected to fail at the sight of him. The bees dropping into the mango's pollen could figure the heart's fall, but they do no act of the situation, so they stay scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the shore grove and the lord of the cool sea

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: addressee from என் நெஞ்சே in line 3

iraicchi.act: the tusker, unable to bear his weary mate's pain, fells a tree to feed her and trumpets in grief
iraicchi.sense: even the elephant on that road cannot bear his mate's suffering, yet the man who crossed it has forgotten the one he left weeping

307.reading: The heroine says the new crescent has already been born, shaped like a broken bangle, appearing slender in the red-mouthed sky as many worship it; alas, have they forgotten, the men who left her weeping for the long wasteland where a tusker, unable to bear the pain of his young female's weary gait, gores and fells a tall yaa tree, takes its white fibre, tastes it with his trunk and looks up trumpeting with a grieving heart?
307.nuance: The crescent counts the months since he left; a broken bangle is also what wasting does to her own wrist.

thinai_evidence.note: he has left across the long wasteland

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: addressee inferred: the colophon gives only the speaker; stage from his journey

308.reading: The friend says that the bond of the man of the great hill, where an elephant, its fearsome head stroked by the curled bud of the grove banana, loses its might and in deluded grief sleeps with difficulty on the slope of falling waters while its tender, weary female strokes its back, has slackened in the hand that gave love.
308.nuance: Lines 1 and 2 are hard to construe (whether the banana bud grieves or strokes, and why the beast loses its might); the female soothing the stricken male could be an iraicchi of the heroine's care, but with the act and its subject unsure it is left as scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the elephant and the man of the great hill

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: addressee inferred: the colophon gives only the speaker; the man is spoken of in the third person

comparisons.vehicle: பெயர்த்துங் கடிந்த செறுவிற் பூக்கும் நின்னூர் நெய்த
comparisons.tenor: the women of his house, who stay though he wrongs them

309.reading: The friend tells the lord that, though the field workers finishing their weeding throw down the fragrant flowers that bees feed on and leave them to wither on the high ridges, the neythal of his town does not say 'they are cruel; we will move to another land', but blooms again in the very field it was weeded from; we are like that neythal, lord: though you do us many unkind things, we cannot do without you.
309.nuance: The neythal is weeded out by the household's own hands and still returns to the same field, which makes the women's loyalty a matter of belonging to the soil rather than of being well treated.

thinai_evidence.note: weeded paddy fields and the field workers

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: addressee from பெரும in line 6; stage from the man's town and his many wrongs

comparisons.tenor: the sky, dimmed and dazed at evening

310.reading: The heroine says the birds have grown lonely, the flowers here have closed, the shore grove is full of loneliness, and the sky too, dazed like us, has turned dim past the day's end; friend, I may yet live in this state if I find someone to tell it to the lord of the cool ford where the cool njaazhal is fragrant.
310.nuance: The evening's loneliness is shared by birds, flowers, grove and sky, and against all of it she sets one practical hope, a messenger.

thinai_evidence.note: the shore grove at the end of day

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: addressee from தோழி in line 5

311.reading: The heroine asks her friend how the gossip can end, when the swift, rattling chariot that would not stop though its driver on the broad fish-smelling ford held it back, whether she saw it or not, was seen by the whole troop of girls plucking the pollen-laden bright flowers of the punnai bent over the high white sand.
311.nuance: 'Whether I saw it or not' gives up her own witness: it no longer matters what she saw, only that everyone else did.

thinai_evidence.note: the great sea and the white sand

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: addressee from தோழி in line 1; stage from the talk about the unmarried pair

comparisons.tenor: the girl at night, one of the man's own
the girl at dawn, one of her family again

312.reading: The man says his beloved is a thief who knows two ways: in the thick of night she comes, filling with fragrance the forest of Mullur of Malaiyan of the red spear and hostile strength, as one of us; at dawn, having shaken out the mixed flowers she wore in her hair and smoothed her sandal-scented locks with oil, her face unmoved, she is as one of her own kin.
312.nuance: The thief steals nothing but herself: the scent she carries at night and the oiled hair at dawn are her two disguises, and the man admires the skill that hides him.

thinai_evidence.note: the forest tryst at midnight

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: addressee inferred: the colophon gives only the speaker; he speaks of 'our beloved' as if to his heart

comparisons.tenor: the friendship, as a knot that cannot be untied

313.reading: The heroine says that with the lord of the shore, where the small white crow of the great sea's edge searches out and eats its prey in the dark backwater of flowing water and roosts in the flower-scented grove, they tied it, and the friendship is tied: it is knotted and settled, hard to untie.
313.nuance: The bird's day ends in a fixed roost after its search; the bond, too, is spoken of as done, in the past tense, beyond anyone's untying.

thinai_evidence.note: the sea crow feeding in the backwater

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: addressee inferred: the colophon gives only the speaker

314.reading: The heroine tells her friend that even in this lonely evening, when the full-bellied cool-voiced cloud from the far high sky flashes bright lightning and the rain comes down darkening everything, he does not come, the man who crossed the wasteland of cruel places, who would come and press her young breasts in embrace.
314.nuance: The rain cloud is a promise kept by the season and broken by the man; the line on her breasts recalls the return she was told to expect.

thinai_evidence.note: the rain cloud at evening

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: addressee from தோழி in line 4; stage from his journey across the waste

comparisons.tenor: the white waterfall pouring down the hill
her shoulders, which turn to him

315.reading: The heroine tells her friend that the man of the high hill, where the white waterfall pours like the rising moon seen over the sea, is like the sun, and her great bamboo-like shoulders are like the nerunji.
315.nuance: The nerunji opens to the sun and follows it, so her shoulders flourish with his presence; but the same sun scorches the dry ground the nerunji grows on, and the pairing does not say which.

thinai_evidence.note: the man of the high hill with its waterfall

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: addressee from தோழி in line 3

316.reading: The heroine asks her friend whether she would live if her mother learned of this sickness-laden distress that loosens her chosen bangles and fills her body with faintness, now that the words of the lord of the shore, where the unceasing sea beats on the sand-heaped shore and the rising waves wipe out the fast-running crab the girls playing at orai point out, have turned to something else.
316.nuance: The waves erasing the crab the girls were following could image his words wiped out, but lines 5 and 6 are unsure and only that one correspondence can be named, a near miss on condition 3.

thinai_evidence.note: the sea shore and its crab

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: addressee from தோழி in line 3; stage from the fear that the mother will learn

317.reading: The friend asks whether the man of the land where the fine dark-grey bull of the wild cattle, beloved of its young cow, eats sweet-sour nelli, sighs hot breath that makes the honey-dripping flowers beside it tremble, and drinks from the green spring of the high hill, will stay away from us in the cold dewy days when the north wind's rain, beyond measure, moves south.
317.nuance: The bull's sour nelli followed by spring water (a taste that turns sweet after the sour) is traditionally read as the hard courtship turning sweet; the beast does nothing of the lovers' situation, so it stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the high hill in the cold dewy season

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: addressee inferred: the colophon gives only the speaker; 'us' includes the heroine

318.reading: The heroine says of the lord of the shore, where fragrant njaazhal and punnai flowers strewn over the gleaming expanse of water alive with attacking sharks make it look like the ground of a frenzy rite, that though he gives no sign, shall she tell anything else to one who knows nothing else even in thought; on the day he embraced these wasted soft bamboo shoulders he swore an unfailing oath, and he himself is the thief, the one bound by it, and the raft that must carry her across.
318.nuance: Thief, debtor and raft are three legal and practical names for one man: he took, he owes, and he alone can save; the word வஞ்சினம், elsewhere a warrior's oath, here binds a lover.

thinai_evidence.note: njaazhal and punnai on the shore

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: addressee inferred: the colophon gives only the speaker; stage from the secret oath

iraicchi.act: the stag clasps its doe and takes shelter with her as the rain-evening comes
iraicchi.sense: even the beasts seek their mates for shelter at the evening of the rains, while the man who should be with her has not come

comparisons.tenor: her body before he ruined its beauty

319.reading: The heroine tells her friend that as the stag, clasping its young doe, shrinks in bewilderment into the bush near the forest, and the good elephant with its trunk joins its female and makes for the dark-sloped hill, the evening has come with the season's great dark rain; if those who ruined her gold-like body's beauty do not come even now, what will become of her sweet life?
319.nuance: The elephant pair repeats the stag's act of sheltering with a mate as the rain-evening comes; the iraicchi is tagged on the stag, and the doubling makes the heroine the only creature left without her partner.

thinai_evidence.note: the rain-season evening

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: addressee from தோழி in line 8; stage from the absent man's promised return

ullurai.tenor: the town's gossip about the heroine and the lord of the shore

pairs.situation: her clean name is made to reek of scandal
the talk spreads through every street of the village
the stuff of the talk is the town's own catch, not anything she did

ullurai.speaker_fit: the heroine uses the drying catch of her own shore, a thing she knows (porul 7.26)

comparisons.tenor: the gossip that sullies her name

320.reading: The heroine says that with the lord of the shore, where the fish the sea fishermen caught, drying with the prawns taken from the backwater, make the moon-white sand reek of flesh as they spread over every dune, they have not even the blame of having laughed together one day, yet this town of the punnai street, by the punnai grove of golden clusters where flowers open and birds call, spreads idle gossip out of its own cruelty.
320.nuance: The drying catch is the town's own trade, and its smell spreads over sand that was clean; the heroine draws the moral without naming it.

thinai_evidence.note: fishermen and their drying catch

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: addressee inferred: the colophon gives only the speaker; stage from the gossip before any meeting

links.note: Kural 1179 says her eyes do not sleep when he fails to come nor when he comes; in Kuruntokai 301 he does not come, and the bell of a chariot that is not there rings in her ear at midnight while her eyes give up sleep.
links.teaches: The poem shows how the couplet's 'when he does not come' still keeps the eyes open: the ear makes his chariot out of the night, so absence is lived as an arrival that never quite happens.

links.note: Kural 1205 rebukes the man for barring her from his heart while he keeps coming into hers; in Kuruntokai 302 the man likewise comes only into her heart at midnight, and she asks whether fear of gossip keeps him away.
links.teaches: Together they give two verdicts on the same phantom visit: the couplet calls it shameless trespass, the poem excuses it as fear of the town, so whether his absence is a fault depends on the reason the heroine allows him.

links.note: Kural 1150 says the town is raising the very gossip they want, since it will bring the lover round; in Kuruntokai 302 the gossip that calls the pair inseparable is what she fears has kept him away. On this reading the same talk helps in one and harms in the other.
links.teaches: The pair shows alar cutting both ways in secret love: the talk the Kural's speaker welcomes as a lever toward marriage can, as the poem fears, frighten a lover into staying away altogether.

links.note: Kural 1171 says the eyes showed him and so she came to see an unending sickness; Kuruntokai 305 opens with the bright fire of love that the eyes brought and follows it to a sickness no one can stop.
links.teaches: The couplet blames the eyes and stops at 'unending'; the poem carries the same sickness to its end in the dunghill cocks' fight that only death stops, so 'unending' is shown to mean ending only in death.

links.note: In Akananuru 91 the friend points to the elephant that shrinks together with its hungry mate on the scorched road as proof that the man still loves; in Kuruntokai 307 the heroine points to a tusker that fells a tree to feed its weary mate as proof that he has forgotten.
links.teaches: The same iraicchi of the tusker's care on the wasteland serves the friend as comfort and the heroine as reproach, so the device's sense is fixed by who is speaking and what she wants, not by the beast.

links.note: Kural 1288 tells the thief that his chest is to her as toddy is to drinkers, though it does them shameful harm; Kuruntokai 309 says the women are like the neythal that blooms again in the field it was weeded from, though he does them many unkind things.
links.teaches: Both say she cannot leave him though he harms her, but the Kural calls the bond an addiction while the poem calls it rootedness in his own field, so the pair shows the same dependence judged as weakness and as loyalty.

links.note: Kural 1222 asks the dim evening whether its partner is as hard-hearted as hers; Kuruntokai 310 sees the sky dazed like herself at day's end and then says she may yet live if someone will carry word to him.
links.teaches: The couplet stops at fellow-feeling with the evening; the poem turns that fellow-feeling into a need for a messenger, so the evening lament is shown as the point where the heroine starts to seek a go-between.

links.note: Kuruntokai 212 has the friend say the shore lord's chariot comes, bells ringing, only to be seen and goes back leaving shame; in Kuruntokai 311 the chariot that would not stop was seen by the whole troop of flower-gathering girls, and the heroine asks how the gossip can end.
links.teaches: Read together, the chariot that the friend in 212 calls mere display is in 311 the very evidence the gossip rests on, so the lover's conspicuous visits are both his courtship and the cause of the alar.

links.note: Kapilar praises Malaiyan in Purananuru 123 as giving more chariots than the raindrops on the heights of Mullur; in Kuruntokai 312, also Kapilar's, the girl comes at midnight filling Malaiyan's Mullur forest with her fragrance.
links.teaches: The same poet uses his patron's hill both as the measure of a king's countless gifts and as the secret ground of a tryst, which shows a court poet setting his love scenes inside the land he praised in puram.

links.note: Kural 1271 has the man tell the girl that though she hides it, her eyes go beyond her control and speak; in Kuruntokai 312 the man marvels that by dawn she is wholly one of her kin again, face unmoved. On the poem's reading her concealment holds.
links.teaches: The pair sets two views of the girl's secret side by side: the Kural's man reads it in her eyes, Kapilar's man admires a disguise he cannot see through, so concealment in kalavu is both a failure and an art.

links.note: Kuruntokai 313 says the friendship with the lord of the shore is knotted and settled, hard to untie; Kuruntokai 304 says the friendship made with the lord of the shore has brought enmity.
links.teaches: Held together they show why 304's grief is so sharp: the bond that 313 praises as impossible to untie is the same bond that, once it brings hostility, cannot be undone either.

links.note: Kural 791 warns that nothing ruins like befriending without inquiry, since for the faithful there is no leaving once the friendship is made; Kuruntokai 313 says the friendship with the shore lord is tied and settled, hard to untie.
links.teaches: The heroine states as her settled joy the very fact the Kural gives as the reason for caution, so the pair shows that love's bond is the friendship the ethics book warns about, entered without the inquiry it prescribes.

links.note: Kar Narpathu 12 has the friend say that his coming is certain, shown beyond doubt by the dark clouds that rise every day; in Kuruntokai 314 the full rain cloud flashes lightning at evening and the heroine says he still does not come. On this reading the sign the friend calls certain has failed.
links.teaches: Set beside the Kar Narpathu's confident friend, the poem shows the other side of the season-sign: the cloud that is offered as proof of return becomes, when he does not come, the measure of his broken word.

links.note: Kuruntokai 202 compares the lover to the nerunji, which first gives a sweet flower and then thorns; Kuruntokai 315 makes the man the sun and her shoulders the nerunji that turns to it.
links.teaches: One weed of poor ground carries two opposite lessons in the same anthology, its turning to the sun as her dependence and its later thorns as his change, so the heroine's image in 315 already holds the pain that 202 states.

links.note: Kural 1288 addresses the lover as thief whose chest is like toddy that harms; Kuruntokai 318 calls the man thief too, but also the one bound by his oath and the raft who must carry her across.
links.teaches: The Kural's 'thief' names only the sweet harm, while the poem turns the same title into a claim: whoever stole is bound to restore, so the word becomes the ground of her demand for marriage.

links.note: Kural 1221 says the hour is not evening but a spear that eats the life of the wedded; in Kuruntokai 319 the rain-evening comes as the stag and the elephant take shelter with their mates, and she asks what will become of her life if he does not come.
links.teaches: The poem shows why the evening kills: it is the hour when every creature goes to its mate, so the Kural's bare claim that evening eats life gets its cause in the paired beasts the heroine watches.

links.note: Kural 1146 says she saw him on one day only, yet the talk has spread like the serpent seizing the moon; Kuruntokai 320 says they have not even the blame of laughing together one day, yet the town spreads gossip.
links.teaches: The Kural concedes one meeting behind the talk while the poem denies even that, so the pair shows the gossip of kalavu needing ever less fact, until in 320 it rests on nothing but the town's cruelty.

source_issues: Kuruntokai colophons give only the speaker (தலைவி கூற்று and the like), so every addressee and stage in thurai_akam is inferred from the poem; each item says so in its note.

301: the base colophon gives குறிஞ்சி and sangamtamil.com gives நெய்தல் (flag); the poem's palmyra and anril support neythal, which is our thinai. This is the only verse in the chapter where our thinai differs from the colophon.
303 lines 1-2: the word வெண்குருகு is split across the line break (வெண்குரு / கு).
306 line 5: பயருங் is doubtful (perhaps பயிரும்); the sense of lines 1-2 is also open, and the verse is marked uncertain.
309 line 1: மாக்கடம் is probably a misdivision of மாக்கள் தம்; line 7 has a stray comma inside a word (நீயெமக், கின்னா).
310 line 6: கமழுஞாழல் is run together (கமழும் ஞாழல்).
314 line 3, 316 line 8 and 318 line 8 were repaired from tamilvu.org; the repairs read correctly.
316 line 6: வாய்ந்த லவன் looks like a faulty division (the crab, அலவன், is clear; the preceding word is not), and the sense of lines 5-7 is uncertain.
320 line 8: தூற்றந்தன் is probably தூற்றும் தன் run together.
